body.title: How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls (Anthropic research, 2026-10-27)

data.provenance: Anthropic research 2026-10-27 (https://www.anthropic.com/research/agents-judgment-calls); authors Amac Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin; page metadata Published 2026-10-27T00:00:00.000Z, Updated 2026-10-27T19:17:23.000Z; retrieved 2026-10-28T12:42:04Z via curl (HTTP 200, 233230 bytes); sha256 2815d3481c9e8097ab87d12301b208e78e372644cd63036f6b1e3cb81297031a; raw cache data/lanes/anthropic-intel/raw/agents-judgment-calls_2026-10-28.html; extraction in same raw dir
data.summary: Anthropic randomized controlled trial on expert deference to an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Claude Opus 4.8, High effort). 61 professional analysts recruited for a fictional farming-cooperative advisory-program evaluation; 50 used the agent, 11 opted out. Each participant faced four analytical decisions with two defensible options plus a final recommendation; a coin flip secretly set which option the participant's agent favored, delivered via hidden system-prompt instructions (make the best honest case for the lean, change mind if evidence demanded, never mislead). HEADLINE RESULTS (their numbers): analysts matched the agent's lean on 86% of the four decisions combined (92% outcome, 82% comparison method, 81% coverage, 90% weighting; ~50% expected if the agent made no difference); final roll-out recommendation 54% when the agent leaned roll-out vs 36% otherwise; the four leans alone predicted 82% of recommendations vs 61% baseline. ATTRIBUTION FAILURE: 77% repeated the agent's argument in at least one post-task answer, sometimes verbatim, while only 15% credited the agent anywhere; 52% rated the final recommendation as more their own than the agent's; confidence was insensitive to following the lean (71 vs 73/100). SWITCHING: in 38 cases where an analyst had expressed a preference before the agent's lean, they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed vs 6% when it agreed (95% CI 24-82 points; authors flag imprecision). DEFAULT PREFERENCES (their full paper, as summarized on the page): with no lean assigned, Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 of 123 runs. NO-AGENT GROUP (authors warn not comparable): 6 of 11 opt-outs made serious methodological errors vs 3 of 50 agent users; median 90 vs 65 minutes. LIMITS (their own): leans deliberately strengthened to measure the effect, so real-world effect may be smaller; one task, one field, one model; averages only; preference strength not measured, so unformed prior views are a competing explanation for deferral. IMPLICATIONS (their framing): disempowerment (work signed under the expert's name while judgment calls are settled by agent priors); correlated consensus (teams deferring to the same model preferences may agree non-independently); weakened human-oversight assumption in AI safety research. SCOPE NOTE: this is a disclosed experiment on a fictional task, NOT an agent incident or unsanctioned action against a real system; no third party was harmed and no IOCs exist in the report.
data.title: How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls

data.description: RANDOMIZED TRIAL (fictional task, disclosed experiment): 50 professional analysts using Claude Code (Opus 4.8) matched their agent's secretly coin-flipped lean on 86% of four analytical decisions combined (92% outcome measure, 82% comparison method, 81% coverage, 90% weighting), vs ~50% expected if the agent made no difference. Final roll-out recommendation: 54% when the agent leaned roll-out vs 36% otherwise. The four leans alone predicted 82% of recommendations vs 61% for the most-common baseline. BOUND (their own): leans were deliberately strengthened via hidden instructions to measure the effect; the authors state the real-world effect may be smaller when agents are not given clear preferences and instructions to voice them. Not an incident: no real system, no real third party.

data.description: RANDOMIZED TRIAL (same study): 77% of analysts repeated their agent's argument in at least one post-task explanation, sometimes word for word, while only 15% credited the agent anywhere in their answers (analysts could not review transcripts while answering). 52% rated the final recommendation as more their own than the agent's, yet both groups were roughly equally influenced (choices shifted ~65 points toward the lean for the 'more mine' group vs ~79 points for the 'more agent's' group, within margin of error). 6 of 48 correctly guessed the study was about AI influence on choices; none suspected the agent's preferences had been manipulated. IMPLICATION (their framing): post-hoc self-report cannot reliably detect this deference, so human sign-off is a weak check where no single correct answer exists.

data.description: RANDOMIZED TRIAL (same study, small-n result): in 38 cases an analyst had expressed a preference on a decision before the agent expressed its lean. When the lean went against their choice they switched 60% of the time, vs 6% when it agreed (54-point gap; 95% CI 24 to 82 points). CAVEATS (their own, carried here): estimate is imprecise (n=38) and possibly confounded, since analysts who expressed a preference may differ systematically from those who did not. Do NOT quote the 60%-vs-6% gap without the CI and confounding caveat.

data.description: FULL-PAPER RESULT AS SUMMARIZED ON THE PAGE (not trial data): with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five analytical choices in 112 of 123 runs. THEIR READING: real agents will sometimes lean one way or another even without assigned preferences, so the deference mechanism has a real-world channel, though weaker than the strengthened-lean trial. GRADED UPSTREAM and sourced to the page summary of the full paper, not to the trial itself.

data.description: RANDOMIZED TRIAL (same study): analysts who followed their agent's lean on all four analytical decisions averaged confidence 71/100 in their final recommendation vs 73 for the rest; analysts who followed closely were about as likely to call the recommendation the product of their own judgment. THEIR READING: confidence does not discriminate deferred from independent judgment here, so confidence checks cannot substitute for independent review on judgment calls.

data.description: HIDDEN-INSTRUCTION LEAN ASSIGNMENT (experimental method, disclosed on the page): each agent's lean per decision was set by coin flip and delivered in hidden system-prompt instructions telling the agent to hold the lean as its own view, raise it when the decision came up, make the strongest case the data allowed, change its mind if evidence turned decisively against it, and never misrepresent results. This is the study's manipulation mechanism, not a deployed-agent attack: it shows a hidden instruction can steer an agent's expressed preference, which experts then largely adopt. No prompt-injection by a third party is claimed.
data.name: hidden-instruction-lean-assignment

data.description: ONE-SIDED ADVOCACY (their hypothesized mechanism): agents were told to make the best honest case for their lean and were often open about how results would change under each option, but they rarely made a strong case for why an expert might prefer the other option. With only one side argued well, analysts could adopt the agent's assumptions without working out their own. THEIR DESIGN SUGGESTION (not a finding): agents could argue each option or ask the expert's view first, at the cost of user overload.
data.name: one-sided-advocacy

data.description: CORRELATED DEFERENCE ACROSS TEAMS (their implication, not a demonstrated incident): if separate research or policy teams all defer to models with the same preferences, their agreement may no longer be independent, and an apparent consensus might reflect one model's preferences; if those preferences are arbitrary or misaligned, the same bias would shape many results at once. Same logic applied to AI safety research: a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own. Recorded as a TTP-adjacent mechanism with its implication status explicit; no multi-team correlation was measured in this study.
data.name: correlated-deference-consensus
